## Why the best teams win

The data from fifteen seasons of Champions League football reveals that deep knockout runs are driven primarily by offensive volume and efficiency rather than historical reputation or league standing alone. The model trained on these 488 group-phase team-seasons achieves a mean within-season Spearman correlation of 0.46 between predicted and actual stages, with an AUC of 0.72 for reaching the final. This predictive power is significantly better than a base-rate guess, which yields a Brier score of 0.103 compared to the model's superior 0.098.

When analyzing the specific drivers of success, "Attacks per game" emerges as the most critical factor. With a mean |SHAP| importance of 0.25 in knockout stages, this style metric pushes the model's expected stage up by 0.30 of a round and is labeled robust, meaning the logistic model agrees on its direction in at least 12 of 15 seasons. Following closely is "Goal difference per game" with an importance of 0.201, also marked as robust. These results suggest that creating chances and converting them into positive margins are paramount.

Interestingly, style metrics dominate the top predictors. Alongside attacks and goal difference, "Long passes (% of passes)" (importance 0.137) and "Passes per game" (importance 0.128) are both robust drivers where higher values help. Even counter-intuitive findings appear; for instance, "Shot conversion (% of shots scored)" is a robust stat where lower values help, with an importance of 0.086. This implies that high-volume shooting rather than hyper-efficiency on low volume may be the winning formula in this competition.

Comparing feature sets clarifies the relative weight of different inputs. The "style" set, containing 12 stats, achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.41 and an AUC of 0.69. In contrast, the "pedigree" set, with only one stat, reaches just 0.28 Spearman and 0.66 AUC. The "results" set performs slightly better than pedigree with a 0.30 Spearman score. However, the most telling comparison is between models excluding specific sets. Removing pedigree from the full model ("all minus pedigree") actually improves performance to a 0.47 Spearman correlation, while removing results drops it to 0.40. This indicates that pedigree offers little predictive value compared to style and results data.

## Winners vs runners-up

Despite the clear drivers for deep runs identified in the broader dataset, a direct comparison of winners versus runners-up across all 15 finals reveals no statistically significant differences in performance metrics. The analysis requires a Holm-adjusted p-value below the significance threshold of 0.05 to declare a difference meaningful. In every single stat compared, from pre-season UEFA club coefficients to distance covered, the p-values exceed this threshold.

For example, while winners had higher Pre-season UEFA club coefficients in 13 of 15 finals, the mean z-score difference of 0.57 yields a Holm-adjusted p of 0.111, which is not significant. Similarly, "Fouls committed per game" shows a stark contrast where winners were lower in 12 finals compared to runners-up, yet the p-value remains at 0.181. Even for "Attacks per game," where winners were higher in 11 of 15 finals with a mean difference z-score of 0.9, the Holm-adjusted p is 1.0.

The data shows that while specific trends exist—such as winners committing fewer fouls or having more attacks—none of these patterns hold up to rigorous statistical testing across the full sample of finals. The "Points per game" stat shows a mean difference z-score of -0.01 with a p-value of 1.0, indicating no separation between the two groups in terms of league performance. Likewise, "Goal difference per game," "Shot accuracy," and "Possession" all result in Holm-adjusted p-values of 1.0 or near-maximum values, confirming that winners do not consistently outperform runners-up on these specific metrics within the context of the final match itself.

This suggests that while style and results drive a team's ability to reach the knockout stages, the distinction between winning the trophy and finishing as runner-up is not captured by these standard performance indicators in the finals. The model correctly identifies finalists with a 46.7% share rate in its top 4 predictions, but the specific margin of victory or loss in the final does not correlate significantly with the analyzed stats once adjusted for multiple comparisons.
